request: Nous aimerions planifier les visites de maintenance chez nos clients, avec une tournée par technicien et une replanification quand un client annule au dernier moment.

problem.value: Planifier les visites de maintenance chez les clients, construire une tournée par technicien et replanifier rapidement quand un client annule au dernier moment. Le besoin sous-jacent probable : réduire les trajets et le temps perdu, et éviter les créneaux techniciens vides ou les visites contractuelles non réalisées.
problem.evidence: « planifier les visites de maintenance chez nos clients, avec une tournée par technicien et une replanification quand un client annule au dernier moment »

current_process.value: Inconnu : planification manuelle, Excel, agenda, autre module ou outil externe ?

existing_solutions.value: Inconnu : outil de planification d'interventions (FSM) ou de tournées déjà licencié, solutions du marché envisagées et rejetées, budget.
existing_solutions.evidence: Non mentionné. La demande part du principe qu'on construit.

success_metrics.value: Inconnu : km ou temps de trajet réduits, taux de visites réalisées, délai de replanification, créneaux récupérés après annulation ?

payer.value: Outil interne pour l'entreprise (le demandeur est le client) ; pas de modèle de revenu à définir.
payer.evidence: « nos clients » : l'organisation planifie ses propres visites.

actors.value: Techniciens (exécutent les tournées), planificateur/dispatcher (probable, construit et ajuste les tournées), client (annule, peut-être via un contact avec un rôle), responsable (approuve éventuellement les changements). À confirmer : qui planifie, qui reçoit l'annulation, qui valide la replanification.
actors.evidence: « tournée par technicien », « un client annule » ; rôles du contexte B2B (manager, client externe, contact).

business_objects.value: Visite de maintenance, Technicien, Tournée (technicien × jour), Client / Contact, Site (adresse d'intervention), probablement Contrat de maintenance. Données à fixer : durée de visite, compétences requises, fenêtre horaire, adresse, origine des visites.
business_objects.evidence: Termes de la demande + objets Contract, Client, Contact, Mission du contexte.

business_rules.value: Inconnu : critères de construction de la tournée (zone géographique, compétences/habilitations, durée, créneaux client, plafond d'heures), définition d'« annulation de dernière minute » (délai), pénalités ou facturation d'une annulation tardive, règles différentes selon client ou contrat (SLA, périodicité contractuelle).
business_rules.evidence: Seul le principe « replanification quand un client annule au dernier moment » est donné.

workflow.value: Cycle de vie probable de la visite : à planifier → planifiée (affectée à une tournée) → confirmée → réalisée, avec branche annulée → à replanifier. À confirmer : où les visites sont créées en amont (récurrence contractuelle, demande client, ticket ?), qui les assigne, quand une visite est « terminée » et ce qui suit (rapport, facturation).

integrations.value: Inconnu : notification des techniciens (canal, mobile), du client (rappel/confirmation, rôle du contact), agenda des techniciens, calcul d'itinéraire/cartographie, lien avec contrats et facturation de la plateforme.
integrations.evidence: Non mentionné ; le contexte rappelle que « notifier » implique qui, quand, quel canal.

permissions.value: Inconnu : qui voit toutes les tournées vs la sienne, qui peut déplacer ou annuler une visite, qui peut forcer une replanification.

config_vs_custom.value: Inconnu : règles de planification identiques pour tous les clients de la plateforme ou paramétrables par client/contrat.

constraints.value: Inconnu : échéance, taille de la flotte de techniciens et volume de visites par jour, droit du travail (temps de conduite et de travail), RGPD sur les adresses et données clients.
constraints.evidence: Non mentionné ; contraintes réglementaires générales du contexte.

edge_cases.value: Annulation très tardive (technicien déjà en route), plusieurs annulations le même jour, aucun créneau de remplacement, technicien absent, visite contractuellement obligatoire à ne pas perdre, client qui annule puis rétablit, deux planificateurs modifiant la même tournée.
edge_cases.evidence: Déduit de « annule au dernier moment ».

reporting.value: Inconnu : suivi des annulations, taux de réalisation, historique des changements de planning. Pas d'obligation d'audit mentionnée.

acceptance.value: Inconnu. Scénario type à valider : un client annule la veille ou le jour même, la tournée est recalculée, le créneau libéré est réutilisé et les personnes concernées sont prévenues.

risks.value: Tournées irréalistes si les durées et distances sont mal estimées, replanifications automatiques qui surprennent les techniciens, adoption par les planificateurs habitués à leur méthode actuelle, données d'adresses incomplètes. Déploiement progressif à définir.

acquisition.value: Outil interne déployé auprès d'un ensemble d'utilisateurs connu (planificateurs, techniciens) : relève du déploiement, pas de l'acquisition.

questions.q: Comment planifiez-vous ces visites aujourd'hui (Excel, agenda, un outil existant ?) et avez-vous déjà un logiciel de planification d'interventions ou de tournées, payé ou non activé, ou des solutions du marché étudiées et écartées ? Y a-t-il un budget ?
questions.why: Acheter ou réutiliser peut supprimer tout ou partie du développement, et le budget dimensionne le reste ; impact élevé et totalement inconnu.

questions.q: D'où viennent les visites à planifier : sont-elles générées automatiquement par les contrats de maintenance (périodicité), demandées par le client, ou saisies à la main ? Et qui les attribue aux techniciens : un planificateur, ou les techniciens eux-mêmes ?
questions.why: Si les visites ne sont créées nulle part en amont, le périmètre s'étend à tout un sous-système de génération et d'affectation ; c'est le principal angle mort.

questions.q: Quand un client annule, que doit-il se passer : le système propose une nouvelle date que le planificateur valide, replanifie tout seul, ou comble le créneau libéré avec une autre visite ? À partir de quel délai une annulation est-elle « de dernière minute » et entraîne-t-elle des conséquences (pénalité, visite contractuelle à ne pas perdre) ?
questions.why: Le niveau d'automatisation de la replanification et les règles associées changent complètement la complexité de la construction.

questions.q: Qu'est-ce qui rend une tournée valable pour vous : zone géographique, compétences ou habilitations du technicien, fenêtres horaires imposées par le client, durée variable selon le type de visite ? Et ces règles diffèrent-elles selon le client ou le contrat ?
questions.why: Ces contraintes déterminent s'il faut un simple tri par zone ou un vrai calcul d'optimisation, et si les règles doivent être paramétrables par client.

questions.q: Combien de techniciens et de visites par jour cela représente-t-il, et qui doit être prévenu (technicien, client via quel contact, canal) lors d'un changement de tournée ?
questions.why: Le volume décide de l'ampleur de l'optimisation nécessaire, et les notifications imposent de préciser qui, quand et par quel canal.

briefs.problem: Maintenance visits at customer sites are planned without a stated, efficient way to build each technician's daily route, and a late customer cancellation leaves a gap that is not obviously recovered.
briefs.solution: A visit-planning module on the existing B2B platform that assigns maintenance visits to technicians, builds a daily route per technician, and handles late cancellations by proposing a rescheduling for a planner to confirm.
introduces: a visit lifecycle (to plan, planned, done, cancelled, to reschedule) distinct from the contract lifecycle
a route-building capability (technician × day) with constraints such as zone, skills and time windows
a rescheduling flow triggered by a late cancellation, which frees a slot and proposes a refill
role-based notifications to technicians and to the right customer contact
concurrent planner edits on the same route and a shared view of technician availability

challenges.headline: Build versus buy planning
challenges.premise: The request takes for granted that route planning and rescheduling must be built inside the platform.
challenges.alternative: Route optimisation and dispatch are a self-contained problem. If a field-service or routing tool is already licensed, or one fits the budget, the build could shrink to a thin link to the platform's customers and contracts. This is reasoning from the scope of the request, not a market claim.
challenges.consequence: Building a route engine, mobile experience and notification layer from scratch could replace a purchased tool at a much higher cost, with no stated budget or deadline to bound it.
challenges.recommendation: Before any estimate, find out what is used today, whether any planning tool is licensed but unused, and which market options were considered and rejected. Fix a budget envelope.

challenges.headline: Where visits come from
challenges.premise: The request starts at planning, as if the visits to plan already exist.
challenges.alternative: Visits could be generated from the maintenance contracts' periodicity, requested by customers, or entered by hand. Starting with manual entry plus planning, and adding contract-driven generation later, keeps the first release bounded.
challenges.consequence: If nothing creates visits upstream, the scope silently grows to a generation and assignment subsystem, including contractually mandatory visits that must not be lost when rescheduled.
challenges.recommendation: Settle the origin of visits and who assigns them before sizing, and decide whether contract-driven generation is in or out of the first release.

challenges.headline: Automatic replanning on cancellation
challenges.premise: A late cancellation triggers rescheduling, without saying who decides or how automatic it is.
challenges.alternative: A suggestion the planner validates (a proposed new date and a candidate visit to fill the freed slot) is much simpler and safer than full automatic replanning. Full automation can be considered once the rules are proven.
challenges.consequence: Automatic replanning can move technicians' days without warning and overturn contract obligations, and it needs a precise definition of 'last minute' that nobody has given.
challenges.recommendation: Start with propose-and-confirm. Define the lateness cut-off, and any consequence of a late cancellation, with the business.

complexity_reasons: route-building rules still unknown (a zone sort versus real optimisation)
rescheduling logic with contract obligations and concurrent edits
notification routing by contact role and technician
scope could expand to visit generation from contracts
risks: Unrealistic routes if visit durations and travel times are estimated poorly or customer addresses are incomplete.
Surprising technicians with automatic changes to their day, or failing to notify the right customer contact.
Losing contractually mandatory visits during rescheduling if the contract link is not modelled.
Planners reluctant to switch from their current method, with no success measure to show a benefit.
Working-time and personal-data constraints on technicians and customer addresses (French labour law, GDPR) that have not been examined.

opportunities.text: Build the visit lifecycle and the cancel-then-reschedule flow as a reusable pattern, similar to the platform's other state-based lifecycles with events and role-based notifications.
Reuse the existing customer and contact roles so that notification routing for visits follows the same logic as the rest of the platform.
Generate visits from contract periodicity once the manual planning flow is proven.

next_steps: Establish how visits are planned today and whether a planning tool is already licensed or affordable, with a budget; decide build or buy before anything else.
Settle where visits originate and who assigns them, and set the first release to manual entry unless contract-driven generation is confirmed.
Define with the planners the rules for a valid route and what counts as a late cancellation, then validate a propose-and-confirm rescheduling scenario with them.
Only then estimate, starting with the volume of technicians and visits per day.

decisions.decision: A human planner remains in the loop for building and validating routes (proposed, to be confirmed by the client).
decisions.why: Rules for routes and cancellations are still unknown, and a validated suggestion limits the harm of a wrong automatic move.
decisions.alternative: Fully automatic route building and replanning.
decisions.tradeoff: More manual effort for planners, in exchange for lower risk and a simpler first build.

briefs.problem: Maintenance visits are planned and rescheduled without a stated, consistent method, so a late cancellation risks leaving gaps in a technician's route and losing a visit that is owed to the client.
briefs.solution: An internal visit-planning tool that builds one route per technician per day from the platform's clients and contracts, and turns a late cancellation into a visit 'to reschedule' with a proposed new slot.
introduces: a visit and route planning model (technician × day) built on existing clients and contracts
a rescheduling flow that keeps a cancelled visit open and proposes a new slot within skill, zone and deadline limits
technician availability, skills and zone management
notifications to technicians and client contacts, routed by contact role
possibly route optimisation (travel times, geographic grouping) as a distinct engine
possibly automatic visit generation from maintenance contract periodicity

challenges.headline: Build before checking what exists
challenges.premise: A custom planning and route tool must be built, with no mention of what is already used or could be bought.
challenges.alternative: If a field-service planning tool is already licensed, or one off the shelf covers routes and rescheduling, integrating it or reusing it avoids building a scheduling engine that is hard to get right.
challenges.consequence: Building route planning and rescheduling from scratch could replicate a paid-for feature and take on a large, ongoing maintenance load.
challenges.recommendation: Before any estimate, inventory current tools and licences, and shortlist two or three market options against the actual needs (routes, last-minute rescheduling, link to contracts).

challenges.headline: Automatic route optimisation by default
challenges.premise: The request implies that the tool itself produces coherent routes per technician and automatically re-plans after a cancellation.
challenges.alternative: A first release could give the planner a visual daily planning per technician, with a cancelled visit moving to a 'to reschedule' list and a suggested slot that checks skills, zone and deadline, without optimising the whole route.
challenges.consequence: Full optimisation is a different order of cost from a planning board. It needs reliable addresses, travel and visit durations, and tends to produce routes technicians reject if the data is poor. The need may not justify it at small volumes.
challenges.recommendation: Get the number of technicians and visits per day, then decide between a planning board with suggestions and true optimisation before scoping.

challenges.headline: Undefined 'last-minute' cancellation
challenges.premise: A late cancellation is treated as a single case solved by rescheduling.
challenges.alternative: Treat cancellation by notice period: far enough ahead, a normal replan; close to the visit, a rule-driven case (contractual deadline, billing or penalty, who picks the slot). These rules may differ by client or contract.
challenges.consequence: Without the notice threshold and its consequences, the rescheduling logic may be wrong for contractual visits, or hard-coded where it should be configurable by client.
challenges.recommendation: Have the business define the threshold, the contractual obligation to reschedule and who chooses the new slot, and check whether it varies by client or contract.

complexity_reasons: scheduling under constraints (skills, zone, time slots, contractual deadlines)
rescheduling rules that may vary by client or contract
possible automatic visit generation from contracts without duplicates
briefs.cost_driver: the scope of route optimisation and automatic rescheduling
risks: Scope can swing from a simple planning board to an optimisation engine depending on answers not yet given.
A tool may already exist or be purchasable, in which case the build duplicates it.
Incomplete client data (address, time slots, contact) would produce unrealistic routes.
Cancellation rules with contractual or billing consequences may be missed until acceptance testing.
Planners and technicians may reject the proposed routes if travel and visit durations are poorly estimated.

opportunities.text: Model the visit as a state-based lifecycle (to plan, planned, confirmed, done, cancelled, to reschedule), reusing the platform's existing lifecycle and role-based notification conventions.
Generate visits from the periodicity of maintenance contracts, once the source of visits is confirmed.
Route notifications to the right client contact using contact roles already held on the platform.

next_steps: Inventory existing and licensed planning tools and shortlist market options; decide build, buy or integrate before any estimate.
Run a short workshop with planners to map the current process, the origin of visits, and the definition and consequences of a late cancellation.
Collect volumes (technicians, visits per day) and whether rules vary by client, to choose between a planning board with suggestions and route optimisation.
If building, ship first a per-technician planning board with a 'to reschedule' list and constraint-checked slot suggestions, before any optimisation.

decisions.decision: A cancelled visit moves to 'to reschedule' rather than being deleted (proposed).
decisions.why: The visit is still owed to the client and may carry a contractual deadline.
decisions.alternative: Delete the visit and create a new one.
decisions.tradeoff: A slightly richer lifecycle in exchange for no lost visits and a cancellation history.

briefs.problem: Maintenance visits at customer sites are not planned in a structured way per technician, and last-minute customer cancellations leave lost slots and unplanned rework (the exact cost and current method are not stated).
briefs.solution: A visit-planning tool that assigns maintenance visits to technician routes and helps reschedule when a customer cancels late. Whether routes are a simple ordered list or an optimised itinerary is still open.
introduces: a visit and technician-route planning model (visit, route per technician per day)
a rescheduling mechanism triggered by cancellation, with its effect on other technicians' routes
assignment rules (skills, zone, availability, time windows) if they apply
a source of visits to plan (contracts, periodicity or manual entry), if it falls within scope
role-based access for planners and technicians, and possibly a mobile view

challenges.headline: Build before checking the market
challenges.premise: A custom planning tool must be built to plan visits, routes and rescheduling.
challenges.alternative: Route planning, technician assignment and rescheduling on cancellation are the core of field-service planning products. Evaluating one against the stated needs first could remove most of the build, leaving only integration with your contracts and customer data.
challenges.consequence: Building route planning and rescheduling from scratch may cost far more than licensing a tool, and the client has not said whether a tool is already owned or budgeted.
challenges.recommendation: Before any design, find out what tool or spreadsheet is used today, whether a field-service licence already exists, and what budget is available. Run a short comparison of two or three off-the-shelf options against the cancellation scenario.

challenges.headline: Route optimisation assumed
challenges.premise: A 'route per technician' implies an optimised itinerary under constraints.
challenges.alternative: A first release could be a daily ordered list per technician with manual drag-and-drop reassignment, with optimisation added only if the data shows a distance or lost-slot problem. This is my proposal, not something the client asked for.
challenges.consequence: Constraint-based optimisation (skills, time windows, travel times, mapping data) is a very different build from a planning board, and it can consume the whole budget before the cancellation case works.
challenges.recommendation: Ask what 'route' means in practice and which constraints must be respected, then decide whether the first release is assisted planning or optimisation.

challenges.headline: Automatic rescheduling by default
challenges.premise: A last-minute cancellation should lead to the visit being rescheduled, apparently without a defined human step.
challenges.alternative: The system could propose options (a new slot, a gap to fill) and the planner validates them. This keeps contract and SLA obligations under human control while the rules are still unknown.
challenges.consequence: Automatic rescheduling without known rules can break contractual maintenance deadlines, move other technicians' days without notice, and create double bookings.
challenges.recommendation: Define 'last minute' and the rescheduling rule with the people who handle cancellations today, and start with assisted proposals.

complexity_reasons: scope ranges from a simple planning board to constrained optimisation
unknown rules that may vary by client or contract
possible need to generate visits from maintenance contracts
briefs.cost_driver: the level of route optimisation and rule handling (simple planning versus constraint-based)
risks: Building something that an existing or purchasable field-service tool already covers, since no tool or budget has been confirmed.
Scope creep toward a full contract and periodic-maintenance subsystem if visits are expected to be generated automatically.
Rescheduling rules that differ by client, contract or SLA, discovered late and requiring configurability.
Technician working-time rules and visit durations that are unknown but constrain any realistic route.
Low adoption if technicians need a mobile view that is not planned for, or if planners keep their spreadsheet in parallel.

opportunities.text: Model visits with an explicit lifecycle (to plan, planned, done, cancelled, to reschedule) so cancellation and rescheduling are first-class states from the start.
Keep assignment rules (skills, zone, time windows) as data rather than code, so an optimiser or per-contract variations can be added later without a rewrite.

next_steps: Establish how visits are planned today and whether a field-service tool or budget already exists.
Compare two or three off-the-shelf tools against the cancellation scenario before committing to a build.
Define with planners what a route is, which constraints apply, and what 'last minute' means, with two or three real cancellation cases.
If building, scope a first release as assisted planning with a validated rescheduling proposal, and set success measures (lost slots, kilometres, contract compliance).
